text: Two ideas today that both come up constantly once your scripts get bigger: scope -- where a variable is actually visible -- and returning more than one value from a function at once, instead of being stuck with just a single answer.

A variable created inside a function is local -- it exists only while that function is running. calculate_total creates line_total, returns it, and then line_total is gone. Try to print it afterward and Python raises a NameError, because it genuinely doesn't exist outside the function anymore. That's a feature: two different functions can both use a variable named line_total internally without stepping on each other.

A variable defined at the top level of your script is global, and reading it from inside a function works fine -- calculate_total_with_tax reads tax_rate without any trouble. But modifying a global from inside a function, like process_order_BAD does with the global keyword, is a well-known source of bugs, because it makes a function's behavior secretly depend on, and change, state outside itself. The better habit, used throughout this course: have the function return a value and let the caller decide what to do with it.

A function can hand back more than one value at once, just by returning a tuple. validate_order returns both whether an order is valid and, when it isn't, why -- False, 'invalid quantity' packs into a tuple behind the scenes, and is_valid, reason equals validate_order of row unpacks it into two separate variables in one line. That's a lot more useful than a function that can only say yes or no.

The same unpacking pattern scales to any number of returned values. summarize_order hands back three things at once -- the order ID, its total, and whether it's valid -- and one line on the calling side, order_id, total, is_valid, captures all three.
Next: modules and packages -- how Python organizes reusable code into files you can import, and how pip install brings in third-party libraries like pandas.
